title: The Owl in the Oak
subtitle: A Bavarian Forest Summer
summary: Mira is ten and spends every summer at her grandfather's small hunting cabin at the edge of the Bavarian Forest, in southern Germany. Deep in the forest there is a very old oak tree, and inside a hollow in the oak there lives an owl. Her grandfather has known this owl for sixty years. Mira does not really believe it can be the same owl. But this summer, her grandfather begins to teach her the sounds the owl makes, and why.

paragraphs: Mira's grandfather lived in a small wooden cabin at the very edge of the Bavarian Forest, in the south of Germany, close to the Czech border. It was a proper Jagdhütte — a hunting cabin — that his own father had built in 1948. It had one room, a stone fireplace, a small kitchen counter, a heavy wooden table, and two narrow beds. There was no electricity. There was a well outside for water. Opa — that was what Mira called him — spent every summer here from May to September. He was a retired forester. He had walked these woods his whole life. Now he was seventy-three and he walked slower, but he still walked. Every day.

Mira was ten. She came to stay with him for four weeks every August. She had done this since she was five. She loved the cabin. She loved the smell of the pine trees. She loved the small wooden bed with the heavy wool blanket. She loved eating supper on the porch at dusk while the swallows dipped over the meadow. She loved Opa, who was tall and quiet and moved through the forest like he owned it, which in a way he did — not the land, but the knowledge of it. He knew every path. He knew every tree that had fallen since he was young. He knew the names of every bird by its song.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: exterior scene. paragraphs: The old oak was two hours' walk from the cabin, deeper into the forest. It was one of the first places Opa always took her when she arrived. He said the oak was probably four hundred years old — perhaps more. It stood in a small clearing where three deer paths met. Its trunk was as wide as Mira's whole family standing in a ring, holding hands. Its branches spread out overhead like a slow-motion explosion. It had been alive when there were still bears in this forest, and wolves, and lynx.

"And it is a special oak," Opa said, on the second day of Mira's visit, as they were walking. "It has an owl. A tawny owl. She lives in the hollow. She has been there since I first came here as a boy. I was six years old the first time my father brought me. That was in 1957. She was there then. She is there now." "Opa," said Mira, patient. "Owls do not live for sixty years. Owls live for twenty years. Maybe." Opa smiled. He said, "Yes. That is what the books say. And yet — I know owls. I have seen many owls in this forest. I have written down their calls. I have watched them raise their young. And the owl in the oak — she is not like the other owls. She has the same voice. She has the same three marks over her left eye. In sixty-eight years. I do not have an explanation for this. I only have what I have seen."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: exterior scene. Mira (10) and Opa stand at the base of an enormous ancient oak tree in a small forest clearing. The oak's trunk is huge — three meters across. About head height there is a large dark hollow. From inside the hollow, the round dark shape of an owl's head just visible. Warm afternoon light filtered through the leaves. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with deep browns and greens.
paragraphs: They came to the clearing. The oak was there. Mira had seen it many times before, but every year she was surprised again by how big it was. She walked around it. She touched the bark. It was rough and warm. Opa waited. Then he pointed up at the hollow. It was at about the height of Mira's head — a dark oval opening in the trunk, deep enough that you could not see the back of it from outside. And inside, sitting still, was a large brown owl. She had the round face and the dark eyes and the small tufts over her ears that Opa had described. And, over her left eye, three small dark markings in a row.

The owl looked at them. She was completely still. She did not seem afraid. She had been looked at by humans many times before. Mira had never been this close to a wild owl before. It was strange to be so close to something so still and so — old. The owl was watching them with a very calm and considered look.

"Do not point at her," Opa said softly. "Owls do not like pointing. They read intent. Just look. You can talk normally. She has heard human voices her whole life. It does not bother her." So Mira did not point. She just stood and looked. She said, softly, "Hello. I am Mira. I have been coming to see you every summer since I was five, though I did not remember. I am ten now." The owl did not react. Owls do not react to what humans say to them. But Mira felt that she had heard.

"Opa," said Mira, very quietly. "Do you really believe it is the same one." Opa thought before he answered. He said, "I do not really know. What I know is: my father showed me an owl in this hollow with three marks over her left eye when I was six. I have looked at that owl every summer of my life since. She has the same marks. She has the same voice. If she is not the same owl — if it is her daughter, or her granddaughter — then somebody has been passing this hollow down for sixty-eight years. Which is also a beautiful thing. But it does not really matter to me which it is. What matters is that when I come here, she is here. And that has been true my whole life. That is what I know. The rest — I do not need to know."

paragraphs: They stayed by the oak until dusk. Opa had brought a small thermos of coffee and a piece of bread. They sat on a fallen log at the edge of the clearing. They did not talk very much. Opa told Mira the names of some of the other birds they could hear in the trees around them. He told her which ones were species that had been in this forest for a long time, and which ones had come recently as the climate changed. He was not sad about the changes. He was matter of fact. The forest was different than it had been when he was young. Some things were gone. Other things were arriving. That was what a forest did.

At dusk the owl came out. She stepped to the edge of her hollow. She stretched. She looked around. Then she opened her wings — huge, silent — and she flew. Mira watched her disappear into the dark trees. She was silent. Owls were built for silence. That was why they could catch things in the dark. Opa said, in the quiet after she had gone, "She hunts all night. She comes back at dawn. Now she will not be back until we are asleep. So we go home. Come." And they walked back to the cabin through the darkening forest, and Mira thought about the owl the whole way.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior scene at the cabin table. Opa (seventies) has a small wooden owl call — a whistle-like tube — in his hand, and is demonstrating it to Mira (10). Mira holds a similar one in her own hands, examining it. Warm afternoon light through the window. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with warm tones.
paragraphs: "Mira," Opa said, the next afternoon at the cabin. "I want to teach you something this summer. I want to teach you the sounds of the owl. Not just so you can hear them. So you can make them. So that you and she can — talk to each other, in a small way. Would you like to learn?" Mira nodded. Opa reached into a small drawer of the wooden table. He took out two small wooden objects — each was a short tube, maybe as long as her finger, with a small hole in one end. They looked like tiny whistles. He gave her one.

"This is an owl call," he said. "My father made them. He carved them from beech wood. He gave me mine when I was eight. Now I am giving you yours. There are three different calls a tawny owl uses. The most famous is the loud territorial call — the one everyone imitates, that goes hoo, ho ho ho, hooooo. That is the male call. The female has a shorter kewick sound. And there is a third one, a low soft trilling, that they only use when they are near each other, calmly. It is not really a call. It is more like — humming. A comfort sound. That one is the one I am going to teach you first."

Opa demonstrated. He put the small wooden tube to his lips. He blew very softly. A small low trilling sound came out — like a purr, but airy. Two notes together, one low and one slightly higher. He held it for maybe three seconds. Then he lowered the tube. He said, "Try." Mira tried. Air came out with no note. She tried again. The note came out too loud, too sharp. Opa did not laugh. He said, "Softer. It is a comfort sound. It is barely a sound at all. Almost like breathing."

She tried again. This time it was better. Not right, but closer. She practiced for maybe half an hour. By the end her lips were tired. But she had made the sound. Opa nodded. He said, "Good. In two days we go back to the oak. In the evening. We will try it with her. We do not know if she will answer. She might. She might not. But we will try."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: exterior scene at dusk in the forest clearing. Mira (10) sits on the fallen log by herself, holding the small wooden owl call to her lips. Opa (seventies) sits at a distance, on another log, watching. The great oak looms in the background. Warm fading light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with deep greens and warm gold.
paragraphs: They went back to the oak two days later. They sat on the log at the edge of the clearing. It was not quite dusk yet — the owl was probably still in her hollow. Opa said, "You do it. I will be quiet. If you get an answer, it is you she is answering, not me. Just try. Do not be nervous. If nothing happens, we come back tomorrow." So Mira sat still. She put the small wooden tube to her lips. She thought about how the call was supposed to sound. She thought about the owl sitting in the hollow, listening to the forest around her, listening to everything at once. Then Mira blew, softly, the low trilling comfort sound.

The forest was quiet. There was no answer. Mira waited. She tried again. Nothing. She waited. She tried a third time. And then, from inside the hollow — she could barely hear it — there was a small answering sound. Low. Airy. Two notes. The same trilling. Mira held her breath. She looked at Opa. Opa nodded very slowly. He was smiling but he was also being careful not to make a big deal of it. He was letting Mira just feel it. Mira looked back at the hollow. She blew the small sound again. And again — soft — the owl answered from inside.

They did this three times. Each time the owl answered. On the fourth try she did not answer. Opa said, quietly, "That is enough for today. Do not overdo it. She has her own life. She has answered enough. She said hello. Now we let her go." Mira agreed. She lowered the tube. She sat still for a while.

They walked back to the cabin. On the way, Mira asked, "Opa. Do you think she knew it was me. Or she just thought I was another owl." Opa thought about this. He said, "She probably thought you were an owl. Or she was not sure and she answered just in case. She does not know it is you. She is an owl. But — and this is the strange part — you are now a person she has talked to. In her whole life, that is a very small number of people. Probably only me, my father, and now you. If she is really an owl who lives for sixty-eight years, that is very few. If she is a young owl who has only been here five years, still very few. Either way — you are one of them now."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: exterior scene at dusk in a different part of the forest near the cabin. Mira (10) sits alone on a log with the owl call, practicing the trilling sound. Small distant birds in the trees. Warm evening light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with deep greens.
paragraphs: For the rest of the summer, Mira practiced. Opa taught her the other calls too — the territorial call, the kewick, and a fourth soft one that Opa said was a mother-owl-to-owlet call, which was mostly used only in spring. Mira practiced them all. She was slow at first. By the end of August she could make all four passably. Not perfectly. But recognizably.

They went back to the oak six more times. Every time Mira tried the calls. Every time the owl answered at least one. Sometimes she answered a lot. Once, in the last week of August, the owl came all the way to the edge of the hollow and sat there looking at them for maybe twenty minutes, exchanging occasional small comfort sounds with Mira. Mira had never sat still that long in her life. When the owl finally flew off to hunt, Mira could barely move. Opa laughed a small laugh and said, "Yes. That is exactly how it feels. Now you know."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior scene at the cabin at night. Opa (seventies) sits in a chair by the stone fireplace, reading. Mira (10) sits on the floor in front of the fire, looking up at him with a serious question. Warm firelight. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with warm gold from the fire.
paragraphs: On the second-to-last night of Mira's stay, Mira asked Opa a question. She had been thinking about it for a while. She said, "Opa. What happens when you can't come here anymore. What happens to the owl. Does someone else come and see her." Opa put down his book. He was quiet for a long moment. Then he said, "I have thought about this a lot, Mira. My father worried about this too. He came here his whole life, and he told me, when he was very old, that he was sad that when he died there would be no one visiting the oak. My father worried that the owl would be — I don't know. Alone. Not that she would be lonely, exactly. Owls are not lonely. But that the — the connection — would break. That she would be a wild owl in a wild forest again, with nobody knowing she was there."

"And what did you do," said Mira. "I promised him I would come. And I did come. Every summer since I was six, I have come. But now I am seventy-three. I have maybe another five or ten years of walking to the oak. Then I will not be able to. Someone else needs to come. That is what I have been thinking. That is why I have been teaching you the calls, Mira. If it is okay with you. If you want to. I would like you to be the next person who visits the owl. Not right now. You are ten. But — for years to come. Maybe — maybe your whole life."

Mira sat by the fire. She was not surprised. She had, in a small way, expected this. She said, "Opa. What if she dies. What if she is really an old owl, and she is really at the end of her life. And she dies. Do I stop coming." Opa smiled. He said, "No. You keep coming. If she dies, there will be another owl. Maybe her chick. Maybe a stranger. Owls take over good hollows. There is always an owl in the oak. There has been for hundreds of years. My father showed me a note in his own father's diary that mentioned an owl in the same hollow in 1918. It was not the same owl. It was probably not even the same family. But it was an owl. If the one we know dies, another will come. You will meet the new one."

"So it is not really the owl," Mira said, slowly. "It is the — the visiting." "Yes," said Opa. "That is exactly right. The tradition is not the owl. The tradition is that someone in the family walks to the oak in the summer, sits with whoever is there, and makes the small trilling sound. That is the tradition. My great-great-grandfather started it, we think, in the 1800s. It has kept going. Small. Quiet. Only one person at a time. But going."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior scene. Mira (10) sitting on the floor by the fire, looking up at Opa (seventies), her face serious and decided. Opa smiles softly. Warm firelight. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with warm gold.
paragraphs: "Yes," said Mira. "I will do it. For my whole life." Opa smiled. He said, "Good. Thank you, Mira. That is a big promise. I will hold you to it." Mira said, "Do I need to teach someone. Later. When I am old." "Yes," said Opa. "You will. You will find someone in the family — maybe your child, maybe your niece, maybe your grandchild — who is the right person. You will know them when you see them. It will feel obvious. Then you teach them the calls. Then, when you cannot walk to the oak anymore, they take over." Mira nodded seriously. She said, "How will I know." Opa said, "You will know because they will be a child who notices small things. The way you noticed the small blue moon lantern — no, wait, that was a different story I read once. You will know because they will be a child who sits still. Who watches. Who does not need to fill silence. Someone like that is very rare. When you find one, you will know."

Mira thought about this. She said, "How did you know I was that person, Opa. I was very small when I first came." Opa thought. He said, "You were four the first time you visited me here. Your parents dropped you off for a weekend. I took you into the forest. You saw a small mushroom on a log. You crouched down and you looked at it for maybe ten minutes. You did not touch it. You just looked. Your mother came to get you and she had to lift you up because you did not want to leave. I knew then. I have been watching you every summer since. I was very patient. I had to be sure. But — yes. It was you. It has been you the whole time. You just did not know yet."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: exterior scene at dusk in the forest clearing. Mira (10) and Opa (seventies) sit together on the fallen log by the great oak. Both are still, both looking at the hollow. The owl sits at the edge of her hollow looking back. Warm evening light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with warm gold.
paragraphs: The last day of the visit, they went one more time to the oak. They sat on the log at dusk. Mira did the trilling sound. The owl answered. They exchanged small sounds for maybe half an hour. Then Mira lowered the tube. She said, quietly, to the owl and to Opa both, "I will come back. I promise." Opa said, "She heard." Mira said, "She is not a person, Opa." Opa said, "I know. But she still heard." And Mira could not argue with that. It felt true.

That night Opa gave Mira a small worn leather book. It was the family diary. He said, "Every visit to the oak, since my great-great-grandfather, has been written in this book. Just one line each. The date and who saw the owl and what she was doing. Some pages are almost blank. Some have hundreds of entries. When your generation takes over, you will write in it too. It is yours now. Keep it safe." Mira took the book. It was very heavy. She opened it. She saw handwriting from many different people, going back to a first page dated 3rd June 1867. She closed it gently. She held it against her chest.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: exterior scene at the small train station in a nearby Bavarian village. Mira (10) stands with a small suitcase and the leather diary held against her chest. Opa (seventies) stands beside her waving. A small red train waits at the platform. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream palette with warm sunlight and muted greens.
paragraphs: Mira went back to visit Opa every summer after that. When she was fourteen, Opa broke his hip and could not walk to the oak anymore. That summer Mira walked alone. She sat on the log alone. She did the trilling sound. The owl answered. Mira wrote in the diary — 12 August 2031. Alone today. Opa's hip. Owl was in the hollow, made the low trill three times. Same marks over the left eye. She brought the diary back to the cabin. She read the entry to Opa. Opa smiled and said, "Good. She is still there."

Opa died when Mira was sixteen. Mira continued to visit the cabin every summer. She continued to walk to the oak. Sometimes the owl was there. Sometimes she was not. In one summer — when Mira was twenty-one — Mira walked to the oak in mid-August and saw the hollow was empty. She went four days in a row. Nothing. She thought — this is it. She has died. She sat by the log and cried a little. On the fifth day, she went one more time. This time a different owl was there. Younger. Smaller. No marks over her left eye. Just a plain young tawny owl, settling in. Mira did the trill. The new owl answered, uncertainly, but she answered. Mira laughed and cried at the same time. She wrote in the diary — 17 August 2038. A new owl in the hollow. She is smaller. No markings over the left eye. She answered the trill on the first try. She is our new owl now. And that was that. And Mira kept going, every summer, for the rest of her life. And someday, she thought, she would find the child in her family who noticed things. And it would begin again.
